claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claims.claim: A single TRPM8 channel can bind up to four ligand molecules.
claims.source: Moreover, based on analysis of channel chimeras with different combinations of wild type and mutated menthol binding sites, it was found that a single TRPM8 channel can bind up to four ligand molecules, each subunit having and ligand binding site with an affinity Kd (in the closed state), and that every bound ligand shifts the equilibrium between the closed and open channel by a similar extent (Janssens and Voets, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Each TRPM8 subunit has a ligand binding site with an affinity Kd in the closed state.
claims.source: Moreover, based on analysis of channel chimeras with different combinations of wild type and mutated menthol binding sites, it was found that a single TRPM8 channel can bind up to four ligand molecules, each subunit having and ligand binding site with an affinity Kd (in the closed state), and that every bound ligand shifts the equilibrium between the closed and open channel by a similar extent (Janssens and Voets, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Every bound ligand shifts the equilibrium between the closed and open TRPM8 channel by a similar extent.
claims.source: Moreover, based on analysis of channel chimeras with different combinations of wild type and mutated menthol binding sites, it was found that a single TRPM8 channel can bind up to four ligand molecules, each subunit having and ligand binding site with an affinity Kd (in the closed state), and that every bound ligand shifts the equilibrium between the closed and open channel by a similar extent (Janssens and Voets, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Excellent fits to the experimental data were obtained when menthol binding acts exclusively by stabilization the open state, while AITC acts by destabilization of the closed state.
claims.source: Importantly, we obtained excellent fits to the experimental data when we set fixed that menthol binding acts exclusively by stabilization the open state, while AITC acts by destabilization of the closed state (Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a result from model fitting with reference to figures.

claims.claim: The model accurately predicts the concentration-dependent effects of AITC and menthol on TRPM8.
claims.source: Gratifyingly, the model accurately predicts the concentration-dependent effects of AITC and menthol on TRPM8, including the mono-exponential time constants in the presence of different AITC concentrations, as well as the bi-exponential relaxation kinetics in the presence of menthol, respectively (Figure 5D,E; Figure 4E,F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a result from model predictions with reference to figures.

claims.claim: AITC represents the first example of a type II TRPM8 agonist.
claims.source: Based on these results, we propose that AITC represents the first example of a type II TRPM8 agonist, acting primarily by destabilizing the closed channel, which contrasts to the Type I agonists, such as menthol, icilin, thymol and linalool, which primarily stabilize the open channel.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the experimental and modeling results.

claims.claim: Type I agonists such as menthol, icilin, thymol and linalool primarily stabilize the open channel.
claims.source: Based on these results, we propose that AITC represents the first example of a type II TRPM8 agonist, acting primarily by destabilizing the closed channel, which contrasts to the Type I agonists, such as menthol, icilin, thymol and linalool, which primarily stabilize the open channel.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the experimental and modeling results.

claims.claim: Application of 50 μM menthol results in slower activation and deactivation kinetics of TRPM8.
claims.source: In line with the above, application of 50 μM menthol results in slower activation and deactivation kinetics, due to the stabilization of the open state (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to a figure supplement.

claims.claim: Addition of 3 mM AITC in the continued presence of menthol resulted in faster activation kinetics, without affecting the time course of deactivation.
claims.source: Addition of 3 mM AITC in the continued presence of menthol resulted in faster activation kinetics, without affecting the time course of deactivation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to a figure supplement.

claims.claim: The combined effects of AITC and menthol are in line with the predictions of the MWC model, assuming that Type I and Type II agonists can act simultaneously and independently.
claims.source: These results are in line with the predictions of the MWC model, assuming that Type I and Type II agonists can act simultaneously and independently, resulting in both stabilization of the open and destabilization of the closed state (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a comparison between experimental results and model predictions.

claims.claim: At a physiological holding potential of −60 mV, 3 mM AITC and 30 µM menthol resulted in comparable steady-state inward current amplitudes.
claims.source: Note that, at a physiological holding potential of −60 mV, these concentrations resulted in comparable steady-state inward current amplitudes (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to a figure.

claims.claim: In response to action potential waveforms, the current in the presence of AITC mainly manifested during the upstroke phase and rapidly deactivates upon action potential repolarization.
claims.source: In response to the action potential waveforms, the current in the presence of AITC mainly manifested during the upstroke phase, and rapidly deactivates upon action potential repolarization.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claims.claim: In the presence of menthol, the peak outward current during action potentials is smaller but a more prominent inward TRPM8 current is observed during the repolarization phase.
claims.source: In comparison, in the presence of menthol, the peak outward current is smaller but a more prominent inward TRPM8 current is observed during the repolarization phase of the action potential (Figure 6A–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claims.claim: Net charge influx during a 1-s train of action potential waveforms at 8 Hz is larger in the presence of menthol.
claims.source: As illustrated in Figure 6D,E, net charge influx is larger in the presence of menthol, whereas net charge efflux is larger in the presence of AITC.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claims.claim: Net charge efflux during a 1-s train of action potential waveforms at 8 Hz is larger in the presence of AITC.
claims.source: As illustrated in Figure 6D,E, net charge influx is larger in the presence of menthol, whereas net charge efflux is larger in the presence of AITC.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claims.claim: Mouse TRPM8 was rapidly activated by AITC.
claims.source: Like its human orthologue, mouse TRPM8 was rapidly activated by AITC, and the difference in gating kinetics in the presence of AITC versus menthol was also observed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to a figure supplement.

claims.claim: AITC-induced current inhibition was much less pronounced in mouse TRPM8 compared to the human orthologue.
claims.source: However, interestingly, AITC-induced current inhibition was much less pronounced in mouse TRPM8 compared to the human orthologue (Figure 7—figure supplement 2): at the end of a 60-s application of 3 mM AITC, mouse TRPM8 current amounted to 88 ± 6% (n = 8) of the peak current, compared to 21 ± 5% in the case of human TRPM8 (n = 7; p=0.00004).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to a figure supplement.

claims.claim: The amplitudes of Ca2+ transients evoked by 60-s-long applications of 3 mM AITC were on average ~30% smaller than those evoked by 30 µM menthol in TRPA1/TRPV1-deficient mouse sensory neurons.
claims.source: In these cells, we found that the amplitudes of Ca2+ transients evoked by a 60-s-long applications of 3 mM AITC were on average ~30% smaller than those evoked by 30 µM menthol (Figure 7A,D).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claims.claim: The peak rate of calcium rise was consistently smaller in response to AITC than to menthol in TRPA1/TRPV1-deficient neurons.
claims.source: Likewise, the peak rate of calcium rise, which represents a measure for the maximal inward calcium current, was consistently smaller in response to AITC than to menthol in neurons (Figure 7A,D).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claims.claim: AITC evoked larger calcium increases and with a higher peak rate of calcium rise than menthol in HEK cells expressing mouse TRPM8.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed an opposite potency of the same concentrations of menthol and AITC in HEK cells expressing mouse TRPM8: AITC evoked larger calcium increases and with a higher peak rate of calcium rise than did menthol (Figure 7B,D).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claims.claim: When action potential firing in TRPA1/TRPV1-deficient sensory neurons was blocked using TTX, a similar ratio of AITC versus menthol responses as in HEK cells was found.
claims.source: Moreover, if action potential firing in the TRPA1/TRPV1-deficient sensory neurons was blocked using tetrodotoxin (TTX; 1 μM), we found a similar ratio of AITC versus menthol responses as in HEK cells (Figure 7C,D), with AITC being slightly more potent than menthol.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claims.claim: Compared to Type II agonists (e.g. AITC), Type I agonists (e.g. menthol) are more potent in evoking calcium influx in excitable cells.
claims.source: Taken together, these data provide further support for the notion that, compared to Type II agonists (e.g. AITC), Type I agonists (e.g. menthol) are more potent in evoking calcium influx in excitable cells, due to enhanced calcium influx during the prolonged inward tail currents following action potentials.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claims.claim: AITC is an atypical agonist of TRPM8, with a mode of action that is fundamentally different from that of all other known TRPM8-activating stimuli.
claims.source: While there are already numerous natural and synthetic agonists known for TRPM8 (Almaraz et al., 2014), our results demonstrate that AITC is an atypical agonist, with a mode of action that is fundamentally different from that of all other known TRPM8-activating stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study with a citation.

claims.claim: Activation of TRPM8 by cooling or by known agonists such as menthol, thymol, linalool, icilin and halothane is associated with a slowing of the kinetics of voltage-dependent channel gating.
claims.source: Activation of TRPM8 by cooling or by known agonists such as the natural compounds menthol, thymol and linalool, and the synthetic agonists such as icilin and halothane, is associated with a slowing of the kinetics of voltage-dependent channel gating (Vanden Abeele et al., 2013; Voets et al., 2004; Voets et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The slowing of the gating kinetics by cooling and known agonists can be explained by a stabilization of the open channel relative to the transition state.
claims.source: This slowing of the gating kinetics can be directly explained by a stabilization of the open channel relative to the transition state, as we illustrated in this work for menthol and elsewhere for cooling (Voets et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Activation of TRPM8 by AITC resulted in an acceleration of the kinetics of voltage-dependent gating.
claims.source: In clear contrast, activation of TRPM8 by AITC resulted in an acceleration of the kinetics of voltage-dependent gating, and we show here that this can be fully explained by a mechanism where AITC leads to a relative destabilization of the closed conformation relative to the transition state.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current work.

claims.claim: The classification of activating ligands as either Type I or Type II may be extended to activating ligands of other voltage- and ligand-sensitive TRP channels.
claims.source: Such classification may also be extended to activating ligands of other voltage- and ligand-sensitive TRP channels.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a speculation about broader applicability.

claims.claim: Activation of TRPV1 by capsaicin or low pH is associated with faster activation time courses upon depolarization, classifying them as Type II ligands.
claims.source: For instance, published current traces suggest that activation of TRPV1 by capsaicin or low pH is associated with faster activation time courses upon depolarization (Aneiros et al., 2011; Voets et al., 2004), classifying them as Type II ligands
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from published data with citations.

claims.claim: The activating effects of PIP2 or lysophosphatidic acid on TRPV1 are associated with slower activation and longer deactivating tails upon repolarization, classifying them as Type I agonists.
claims.source: whereas the activating effects of phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) or lysophosphatidic acid are associated with slower activation and longer deactivating tails upon repolarization, classifying them a Type I agonists (Nieto-Posadas et al., 2012; Ufret-Vincenty et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from published data with citations.

claims.claim: Type II ligands such as AITC reduce the difference Gibbs free energy between the closed state and the transition state (ΔGα†), without affecting the difference Gibbs free energy between the open state and the transition state (ΔGβ†).
claims.source: Indeed, our results indicate that Type II ligands such as AITC reduce the difference Gibbs free energy between the closed state and the transition state (ΔGα†), without affecting the difference Gibbs free energy between the open state and the transition state (ΔGβ†).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: The AITC-induced conformational change at its binding site occurs early in the gating process, prior to the main close-open transition.
claims.source: This suggests that the AITC-induced conformational change at its binding site occurs early in the gating process, prior to the main close-open transition.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from the thermodynamic analysis.

claims.claim: Type I ligands such as menthol cause an increase in ΔGβ†, without affecting ΔGα†.
claims.source: Oppositely, Type I ligands such as menthol cause an increase in ΔGβ†, without affecting ΔGα†.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: The menthol-induced conformational change at its binding sites occurs later than the main close-open transition.
claims.source: This indicates that the menthol-induced conformational change at its binding sites occurs later than the main close-open transition.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from the thermodynamic analysis.

claims.claim: For menthol binding to TRPM8, a kon of 0.55 μM−1s−1 was obtained.
claims.source: For example, for menthol binding we obtained a kon of 0.55 μM−1s−1, which is well below the diffusion-limited rate (>100 μM−1s−1), and also one order of magnitude or more lower than binding rates for ligands to synaptic ligand-gated channels, such as the ionotropic receptors for glutamate (kon≈ 5 μM−1s−1) (Clements and Westbrook, 1991), ATP (kon≈ 12 μM−1s−1) (Bean, 1990) or acetylcholine (kon≈ 60 μM−1s−1) (Sine et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a result from kinetic fits with citations for comparison.

claims.claim: The binding site for menthol is located in a hydrophobic domain in between the transmembrane helices.
claims.source: Indeed, whereas binding sites for glutamate, ATP and acetylcholine are located extracellularly (Hille, 2001), directly accessible from the aqueous phase, the binding site for menthol is located in a hydrophobic domain in between the transmembrane helices (Bandell et al., 2006; Voets et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The observation that current relaxation time courses of TRPM8 in the presence of menthol become multi-exponential is a direct consequence of the slow equilibration rate of menthol with its binding site in comparison to the transition rates between closed and open channel conformations.

results.result: AITC activates TRPM8 in a subset of TRPV1/TRPA1-deficient DRG neurons. Approximately 9% of TRPV1/TRPA1-deficient neurons responded to 3 mM AITC, and 98% of these AITC-responsive neurons also responded to menthol. Both responses were fully inhibited by the TRPM8 antagonist AMTB, demonstrating that TRPV1- and TRPA1-independent AITC responses depend on TRPM8.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C20 provide converging evidence from calcium imaging experiments in knockout neurons showing AITC responses that are menthol-sensitive and AMTB-inhibitable. The use of genetic deletion controls (TRPV1/TRPA1 knockout) and pharmacological antagonism (AMTB) provides strong support for TRPM8-mediated AITC responses.

results.result: AITC directly activates heterologously expressed human TRPM8 in a membrane-delimited manner. AITC at concentrations ≥300 μM caused rapid and reversible increases in TRPM8 current in whole-cell recordings and inside-out patches. The effect was concentration-dependent but did not saturate at 10 mM. TIRF imaging showed no detectable change in membrane TRPM8 levels, and the rapid onset (~2 s) excludes trafficking as a mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C27 provide multiple lines of evidence including whole-cell electrophysiology, inside-out patch recordings, and TIRF imaging. The inside-out patch data (C24-C25) definitively establish membrane-delimited action, and TIRF imaging (C26-C27) rules out trafficking. The rapid kinetics and concentration-dependence are well-documented.

results.result: AITC shifts the voltage-dependent activation of TRPM8 toward more negative voltages in a concentration-dependent manner without affecting maximal conductance at strongly depolarizing potentials.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 describe steady-state conductance analysis from voltage-step protocols (Figure 3). The leftward shift in activation curves is a standard measure of agonist effect on voltage-gated channels and is clearly demonstrated with appropriate controls and concentration-dependence.

results.result: AITC and menthol have opposite effects on TRPM8 gating kinetics. AITC accelerates activation kinetics upon depolarization while maintaining mono-exponential relaxation, whereas menthol slows both activation and deactivation kinetics, producing bi-exponential relaxation. Other known agonists (thymol, icilin, linalool) act similarly to menthol.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C35 describe detailed kinetic analysis with exponential fitting to current traces. The differential effects are clearly shown in Figure 4 with appropriate quantification. The mono- vs bi-exponential distinction is rigorously demonstrated with residual analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The extension to other agonists (C35) provides additional support.

results.result: AITC and menthol represent two distinct types of TRPM8 agonists with fundamentally different mechanisms. Type I agonists (menthol-like) stabilize the open channel, producing slowly deactivating tail currents. Type II agonists (AITC-like) destabilize the closed channel, accelerating activation without affecting deactivation kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 and C36-C41 establish the classification framework based on the kinetic data. The mechanistic interpretations (C38-C41) logically follow from the observed kinetic effects: slow tail currents indicate impeded deactivation (open state stabilization), while faster activation indicates facilitated opening (closed state destabilization). This is a major conceptual contribution.

results.result: A voltage-dependent MWC model accurately reproduces the differential effects of Type I and Type II agonists when menthol acts exclusively by stabilizing the open state and AITC acts by destabilizing the closed state. The model predicts concentration-dependent effects including mono-exponential kinetics for AITC and bi-exponential kinetics for menthol.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 describe model fitting results shown in Figure 5. The excellent fits to experimental data (C45) and accurate predictions of concentration-dependent effects (C46) provide strong quantitative support. The model parameters are provided in Table 1. This represents rigorous biophysical modeling that validates the mechanistic framework.

results.result: Type I and Type II agonists can act simultaneously and independently on TRPM8. Application of AITC in the presence of menthol produces faster activation kinetics without affecting deactivation, consistent with MWC model predictions for simultaneous stabilization of the open state and destabilization of the closed state.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 describe experiments testing combined agonist effects (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). The results match model predictions for independent action, providing additional validation of the mechanistic framework. This demonstrates that the two agonist types act at distinct sites or through distinct mechanisms.

results.result: Type I and Type II agonists have distinct impacts on TRPM8 currents during action potentials. At equipotent concentrations, AITC produces larger outward currents during depolarization with rapid deactivation, while menthol produces smaller outward currents but larger inward currents during repolarization. Net charge influx is larger with menthol, while net charge efflux is larger with AITC.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 and C52-C56 describe action potential clamp experiments (Figure 6). The differential effects on charge movement are clearly demonstrated and quantified. This extends the kinetic findings to physiologically relevant voltage waveforms, showing functional consequences of the different agonist mechanisms.

results.result: Mouse TRPM8 is rapidly activated by AITC with similar kinetic differences between AITC and menthol as human TRPM8, but AITC-induced current inhibition is much less pronounced in mouse TRPM8 (88% remaining current) compared to human TRPM8 (21% remaining current) after 60 s exposure to 3 mM AITC.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 describe species differences in AITC responses (Figure 7—figure supplement 1-2). The data clearly show conserved activation mechanisms but different inhibition profiles. Sample sizes are adequate (n=7-8) and statistical significance is reported (p=0.00004). This is an important observation for interpreting in vivo mouse studies.

results.result: Type I agonists are more potent than Type II agonists in evoking calcium influx in excitable cells. In TRPA1/TRPV1-deficient neurons, menthol evoked larger Ca2+ transients and higher peak rates of calcium rise than AITC. This difference was abolished by TTX, and the opposite pattern was observed in non-excitable HEK cells, demonstrating that Type I agonists are more effective due to enhanced calcium influx during prolonged inward tail currents following action potentials.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 describe calcium imaging experiments comparing neurons and HEK cells with and without TTX (Figure 7). The reversal of relative potency by TTX provides strong evidence that the differential effects depend on action potential firing. This is a key physiological consequence of the different agonist mechanisms and is well-controlled.

results.result: AITC is an atypical TRPM8 agonist with a fundamentally different mode of action from all other known TRPM8-activating stimuli. While cooling and known agonists (menthol, thymol, linalool, icilin, halothane) slow gating kinetics through open state stabilization, AITC accelerates gating kinetics through closed state destabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 synthesize the findings and place them in context of prior work on TRPM8 activation. The contrast with all previously characterized agonists is clearly established through both current data and citations. This represents a major conceptual advance in understanding TRPM8 pharmacology.

results.result: Type II ligands reduce the Gibbs free energy difference between closed state and transition state (ΔGα†) without affecting ΔGβ†, suggesting AITC-induced conformational changes occur early in gating before the main close-open transition. Type I ligands increase ΔGβ† without affecting ΔGα†, suggesting menthol-induced conformational changes occur after the main close-open transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 provide thermodynamic interpretation of the kinetic data. The reasoning follows standard transition state theory and is consistent with the observed effects on opening vs closing rates. This provides mechanistic insight into the timing of ligand-induced conformational changes during the gating cycle.

results.result: Menthol binding to TRPM8 has a kon of 0.55 μM⁻¹s⁻¹, which is well below diffusion-limited rates and slower than ligand binding to synaptic receptors. This slow equilibration rate, attributed to the hydrophobic transmembrane location of the menthol binding site, explains the multi-exponential relaxation kinetics observed in the presence of menthol.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 describe kinetic parameters obtained from model fitting (Table 1) and provide mechanistic interpretation. The comparison to other receptors (with citations) contextualizes the findings. The explanation for multi-exponential kinetics based on slow ligand equilibration is mechanistically sound and consistent with the structural location of the binding site.

results.result: During action potentials, AITC-induced TRPM8 current manifests mainly during the upstroke phase with rapid deactivation, while menthol produces less outward current but more prominent inward current during repolarization, leading to more Ca2+ influx. Inhibiting action potential firing with TTX has a more profound effect on menthol-induced responses than AITC-induced responses in sensory neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 describe the physiological consequences of differential gating kinetics. The action potential clamp data (Figure 6) and TTX experiments (Figure 7) provide direct experimental support. This demonstrates the functional importance of the mechanistic differences between agonist types.

results.result: TRPM8 mediates residual TRPA1- and TRPV1-independent AITC responses in mouse sensory neurons, but only at high concentrations (≥300 μM). TRPM8 is ~100-fold less sensitive to AITC than TRPA1 but comparable to TRPV1. AITC concentrations ≤100 μM evoke strictly TRPA1-dependent responses, while higher concentrations can activate TRPV1 or TRPM8.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C86 establish the concentration-dependence and relative potency of AITC at different TRP channels. The data are consistent with prior literature (cited) and explain the residual responses in knockout neurons. This provides important context for interpreting AITC experiments in vivo.

results.result: In vivo AITC experiments typically use 10-100 mM concentrations, which may activate TRPM8-positive sensory nerve endings in addition to TRPA1 and TRPV1. Since TRPM8 activation can cause analgesia, this may complicate interpretation of AITC pain studies. Consistent with this, 100 mM AITC transiently increased cold sensitivity in human volunteers.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C91 discuss implications for in vivo studies with appropriate citations. The speculation about TRPM8 involvement (C89) is reasonable given the concentration-response data. The human volunteer data (C91, cited) provides supporting evidence. This is important for the field but represents interpretation rather than new experimental findings.

results.result: The Type I/Type II classification may extend to other voltage- and ligand-sensitive TRP channels. Published data suggest capsaicin and low pH act as Type II ligands on TRPV1 (faster activation), while PIP2 and lysophosphatidic acid act as Type I agonists (slower activation, longer tails).
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 propose extension of the classification framework to other TRP channels based on published current traces. While the reasoning is sound and citations are provided, this represents reinterpretation of prior data rather than new experiments. The classification would require systematic kinetic analysis similar to that performed here for TRPM8 to be definitively established.

results.result: A single TRPM8 channel can bind up to four ligand molecules (one per subunit), each with affinity Kd in the closed state, and every bound ligand shifts the closed-open equilibrium by a similar extent.
results.evaluation: Claim C42-C44 cite prior work (Janssens and Voets, 2011) establishing these properties through chimera analysis. This is background information used to build the MWC model and is appropriately attributed to prior work.

results.result: This study demonstrates for the first time the existence of two types of agonists with distinct state-dependent effects for a TRP channel. Similar classification has been used for decades in voltage-gated Na+, K+, and Ca2+ channels, where mechanistic insight has been key to understanding physiological impact. Establishing state-dependent modes of action will be essential for understanding TRP channel pharmacology and conformational changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 place the work in broader context with appropriate citations. Claim C94 accurately states this is the first such demonstration for TRP channels. Claim C95 is a forward-looking statement about the importance of this approach, which is reasonable given the demonstrated utility in other channel families.

results.result: Background on TRP channels and AITC: TRP channels act as polymodal sensors of temperature and chemicals. Capsaicin activates TRPV1, menthol activates TRPM8, and AITC (found in mustard/wasabi at 5-30 mM) activates TRPA1 and TRPV1. Approximately 10% of DRG neurons remain AITC-responsive after TRPA1/TRPV1 deletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C15 provide background information with appropriate citations to prior literature. These establish the context and motivation for the study. The information is accurately represented and properly attributed.
